sec.t:
प्लेटें करीब उतनी ही तेज़ी से खिसकती हैं जितनी से तुम्हारे नाख़ून बढ़ते हैं, साल में कुछ सेंटीमीटर। जहाँ दो प्लेटें मिलती हैं, एक दरार के साथ-साथ जिसे भ्रंश या फ़ॉल्ट कहते हैं, वहाँ उनके खुरदुरे किनारे एक-दूसरे को जकड़ लेते हैं। हर प्लेट का बाकी हिस्सा चलता रहता है, इसलिए फ़ॉल्ट के पास की चट्टान मुड़ने लगती है, जैसे एक सिरे से बगल में धकेला गया फुटा।

आख़िर में चट्टान और नहीं मुड़ पाती। वह टूटती है और फिसल जाती है, कभी-कभी कुछ ही सेकंडों में कई मीटर। जमा हुई ऊर्जा ज़मीन में तरंगों के रूप में बाहर की ओर दौड़ती है। यही वह झटका है जो तुम महसूस करते हो।

कैलिफ़ोर्निया में दो प्लेटें सैन एंड्रियास फ़ॉल्ट के साथ-साथ एक-दूसरे के बगल से सरकती हैं। 1906 में वहाँ एक फिसलन ने [[@san-francisco|सैन फ़्रांसिस्को]] को हिला दिया, और उसके बाद लगी आगों ने शहर का बड़ा हिस्सा तबाह कर दिया। भारत में, भारत को ढोने वाली प्लेट आज भी एशिया में धँस रही है, [[@himalaya-form|हिमालय]] को उठा रही है और चट्टानों को तब तक भींच रही है जब तक वे चटक न जाएँ।

सिस्मोमीटर ज़मीन के हिलने को टेढ़ी-मेढ़ी लकीरों के रूप में दर्ज करते हैं। वैज्ञानिक तरंगों के आकार से भूकंप की तीव्रता निकालते हैं। सबसे पहले पहुँचने वाली तरंगें, जिन्हें P तरंगें कहते हैं, चट्टान को धकेलती और खींचती हैं। धीमी S तरंगें उसे अगल-बगल हिलाती हैं, और आम तौर पर ज़्यादा नुकसान करती हैं।

पैमाने पर हर दर्जा ऊपर जाने का मतलब है लगभग 32 गुना ज़्यादा [[energy|ऊर्जा]]। तीव्रता 7 का भूकंप तीव्रता 6 वाले से थोड़ा-सा ताकतवर नहीं होता। वह बिल्कुल अलग ही दर्जे का होता है। अब तक दर्ज सबसे बड़ा भूकंप, 1960 में चिली में, 9.5 का था। भारत का राष्ट्रीय भूकंप विज्ञान केंद्र देश भर में स्टेशन चलाता है और हर भूकंप की ख़बर कुछ ही मिनटों में देता है।

26 जनवरी 2001 की सुबह, जब लोग गणतंत्र दिवस के लिए इकट्ठा हो रहे थे, गुजरात के भुज में 7.7 तीव्रता का भूकंप आया। बहुत-सी इमारतें ढह गईं, और पूरे [[@gujarat-rann|कच्छ]] के क़स्बों को भारी नुकसान हुआ। इसके बाद गुजरात ने निर्माण के और कड़े नियमों के साथ फिर से बसावट की, और आज भुज का उबरना एक मिसाल के तौर पर पढ़ा जाता है।

1950 में इससे भी बड़ा, 8.6 तीव्रता का भूकंप असम और तिब्बत में आया। इसने नदियों के रास्ते बदल दिए और पहाड़ियों में जगह-जगह [[@landslides|भूस्खलन]] कर दिए।

भारत का भूकंप नक्शा देश को इस हिसाब से ज़ोन में बाँटता है कि ज़मीन कितनी ज़ोर से हिल सकती है। दिल्ली ज़्यादा ख़तरे वाले ज़ोन में है। हिमालय का बड़ा हिस्सा, कच्छ और पूर्वोत्तर सबसे ऊँचे ज़ोन में हैं, इसलिए वहाँ की इमारतों को सबसे कड़े नियम मानने पड़ते हैं।

{{story:skyscrapers}}

ज़मीन हिले तो: नीचे झुको, किसी मज़बूत मेज़ के नीचे छिपो, और उसे पकड़े रहो। खिड़कियों से दूर रहो। मज़बूत इमारतें और अभ्यास जानें बचाते हैं।

ज़्यादातर चोटें चीज़ों के गिरने या इमारतों के ढहने से लगती हैं, ज़मीन से नहीं। इसीलिए [[engineer|इंजीनियर]] इमारतों को ऐसा बनाते हैं कि वे झूलें पर टूटें नहीं। जापान और अमेरिका की कुछ [[@skyscrapers|गगनचुंबी इमारतें]] रबर के विशाल गद्दों पर टिकी हैं, या उनके ऊपरी हिस्से में बड़े-बड़े झूलते वज़न लगे हैं जो झूलने को काट देते हैं। भूकंप वाले इलाकों के स्कूल अभ्यास करवाते हैं, ताकि सबको बिना सोचे पता हो कि क्या करना है।

भूकंप की तरंगें पूरी धरती के आर-पार जाती हैं। दुनिया भर के स्टेशनों पर इनके पहुँचने का समय नापकर वैज्ञानिकों ने पता लगाया कि [[@inside-earth|धरती के अंदर क्या है]]।

कुछ जानवर शायद पहली, तेज़ तरंगों को उस तेज़ झटके से कुछ सेकंड पहले भाँप लेते हैं, जो इंसान महसूस करते हैं। मसलन हाथी अपने पैरों से [[vibration|कंपन]] पकड़ सकते हैं, हालाँकि किसी ने यह साबित नहीं किया कि जानवर कई दिन पहले भूकंप का अंदाज़ा लगा सकते हैं।

text: एल नीनो और ला नीना [[tropical|उष्णकटिबंधीय]] प्रशांत महासागर के दो उलटे मिज़ाज हैं। ये हर कुछ साल में बारी-बारी से बदलते रहते हैं, और दुनिया के बहुत-से हिस्सों का मौसम बदल देते हैं।

आम तौर पर [[equator|भूमध्य रेखा]] के साथ-साथ पूरब से पश्चिम की ओर लगातार हवाएँ चलती हैं, जिन्हें [[@wind-patterns|व्यापारिक पवनें]] कहते हैं। ये ऊपर के गर्म पानी को इंडोनेशिया और ऑस्ट्रेलिया की ओर धकेलती हैं, जबकि पेरू के तट के पास गहराई से ठंडा पानी ऊपर उठता है। एल नीनो में व्यापारिक पवनें कमज़ोर पड़ जाती हैं। गर्म पानी वापस पूरब की ओर फैलता है, और पूर्वी प्रशांत असामान्य रूप से गर्म हो जाता है। ला नीना में व्यापारिक पवनें आम से ज़्यादा ज़ोर से चलती हैं, और पूर्वी प्रशांत ठंडा हो जाता है।
वैज्ञानिक इस पूरे चक्र को ENSO कहते हैं, जो एल नीनो–दक्षिणी दोलन का छोटा रूप है।

sec.t:
पेरू के तट के मछुआरों ने बहुत पहले देखा कि हर कुछ साल में क्रिसमस के आसपास समुद्र गर्म हो जाता है और मछलियाँ कम मिलती हैं। उन्होंने इसे एल नीनो कहा, जो [[@spanish-language|स्पैनिश]] में "लड़का" है, यानी बाल यीशु। ठंडे उलटे दौर को बाद में ला नीना, "लड़की", नाम मिला।

मछलियों के ग़ायब होने की एक वजह है। पेरू के पास गहराई से उठता ठंडा पानी [[nutrient|पोषक तत्व]] लाता है, जो प्लवक को खिलाते हैं, और प्लवक एंचोवी मछलियों के विशाल झुंडों को। एल नीनो में गर्म पानी समुद्र पर ढक्कन की तरह बैठ जाता है और ठंडे पानी का ऊपर उठना रोक देता है। 1972–73 में एंचोवी की पकड़ धड़ाम से गिर गई, जिससे [[@fishing-boats|मछली पकड़ने वाली नावों]] को और दुनिया भर के उन किसानों को नुकसान हुआ जो जानवरों के चारे में मछली का चूरा इस्तेमाल करते थे।

sec.h: भारत और अमेरिका पर इसका असर
sec.t:
एल नीनो वाले साल अक्सर भारत में कमज़ोर [[@monsoon|मानसून]] और [[@droughts|सूखे]] का ज़्यादा ख़तरा लाते हैं। कुछ सबसे सूखे साल, जैसे 2009 और 2015, एल नीनो के दौरान आए। ला नीना वाले सालों में अक्सर अच्छी बारिश होती है। पर एल नीनो बस एक खिलाड़ी है। हिंद महासागर के तापमान का एक पैटर्न, जिसे इंडियन ओशन डाइपोल कहते हैं, इसके असर को बढ़ा भी सकता है और काट भी सकता है।

अमेरिका में एल नीनो वाली सर्दियाँ दक्षिण में, कैलिफ़ोर्निया से फ़्लोरिडा तक, ज़्यादा गीली और उत्तर में हल्की होती हैं। ला नीना अक्सर दक्षिण-पश्चिम में सूखा लाती है। ला नीना वाले सालों में अटलांटिक में [[@hurricanes|हरिकेन]] भी ज़्यादा आते हैं, क्योंकि समुद्र के बहुत ऊपर हवाएँ शांत रहती हैं और तूफ़ानों को बढ़ने देती हैं।

एल नीनो ऑस्ट्रेलिया और इंडोनेशिया में सूखा और जंगलों की आग ला सकता है, और पेरू के आम तौर पर सूखे तट पर बाढ़।

आज NOAA और दूसरी एजेंसियाँ तैरते बोयों, समुद्री रोबोटों और [[@satellites-help|उपग्रहों]] के जाल से प्रशांत पर नज़र रखती हैं। वे हर दिन पानी का तापमान और हवाएँ नापते हैं। [[@supercomputers|कंप्यूटर मॉडल]] इन आँकड़ों से कई महीने पहले एल नीनो या ला नीना का पूर्वानुमान लगाते हैं, जिससे भारत के किसानों को यह तय करने में मदद मिलती है कि क्या और कब बोना है।

एल नीनो कुछ समय के लिए पूरी धरती को थोड़ा गर्म भी कर देता है, क्योंकि [[@ocean-and-climate|समुद्र में जमा गर्मी]] हवा में निकल आती है। लंबे समय से बढ़ती गर्मी के ऊपर ताकतवर एल नीनो ने 2016 और 2023 को अब तक दर्ज सबसे गर्म सालों में से दो बनाने में हाथ बँटाया।

text: Most scientists think yes. Europa, one of Jupiter's four largest moons, is covered in a shell of ice. Beneath it, there is very probably a deep ocean of salty liquid water. Estimates suggest it could hold about twice as much water as all of Earth's oceans.

Nobody has seen this ocean, but several clues point to it. Europa's surface is smooth, young and criss-crossed with cracks, as if the ice floats and shifts. Its magnetic signals behave as if a salty liquid lies underneath. And Jupiter's [[gravity|gravity]] squeezes Europa enough to keep water warm inside.
That makes Europa one of the best places in the [[solar-system|solar system]] to search for life beyond Earth.

st.prompt: Europa is about 780 million km from the Sun, far too cold for liquid water at the surface. What keeps its ocean from freezing solid?

options.t: Jupiter's gravity squeezes and stretches it, making heat
Sunlight shines through the ice and warms it
Europa has a hot atmosphere that traps heat

st.reveal: As Europa orbits, Jupiter's huge gravity pulls on it more strongly at some points than others, flexing the moon like a squeezed stress ball. That constant flexing makes heat inside, enough to keep a deep ocean liquid under the ice.

src: NASA and Jet Propulsion Laboratory, Europa Clipper mission.
NASA, Galileo mission to Jupiter (1989–2003).
European Space Agency, JUICE mission.
n.certNote: Several strong lines of evidence point to a salty ocean under Europa's ice, but nobody has seen it directly. Estimates of how thick the ice is range from a few kilometres to more than 25 km.

d.try: Squeeze and release a rubber ball or a ball of play dough quickly in your hand for a minute, then hold it to your cheek. It feels a little warmer. Jupiter squeezes Europa in a similar way, over and over, and that flexing helps keep its ocean liquid.
myth: Scientists have found life on Europa.
No life has been found on Europa, or anywhere beyond Earth. Europa is a top place to look because it seems to have water, chemicals and energy, but missions so far can only study it from a distance.
facts: about 3,100 km wide, a little smaller than our Moon
probably about 15–25 km thick, though estimates vary

sec.t:
In January 1610, [[@galileo|Galileo]] pointed his small telescope at Jupiter and saw four little points of light that moved around it night after night. They were moons, the first ever found circling another planet. Europa is one of them, alongside Io, Ganymede and Callisto.

Europa is slightly smaller than our own Moon. Its surface is mostly water ice, brighter than fresh snow in places, and streaked with reddish-brown lines. Some of those streaks may contain salts that have come up from below.

Europa is about five times further from the Sun than Earth is. Its surface is around −160 °C at the [[equator|equator]] and colder near the poles. So why isn't its ocean frozen?

The answer is tidal heating. Europa's [[orbit|orbit]] is slightly stretched, so its distance from [[@jupiter-giant|Jupiter]] keeps changing. The giant planet's gravity pulls harder when Europa is close and less when it is far, flexing the moon over and over. On Earth, the Moon's pull raises [[@tides|tides]] in the sea. On Europa, Jupiter's pull bends the whole moon, and that bending makes heat.

Life on Earth needs liquid water, the right chemicals and a source of energy. Europa may have all three. Its ocean probably sits on a rocky sea floor. On Earth, [[@geysers-hot-springs|hot springs]] on the ocean floor, called [[@deep-sea-vents|deep-sea vents]], support whole communities of animals in total darkness. Something similar might happen on Europa.

That doesn't mean life is there, only that it is worth checking. In October 2024, NASA launched Europa Clipper, the largest spacecraft NASA has ever built for a planetary mission. It should reach Jupiter in 2030 and fly past Europa dozens of times, measuring the ice, the ocean and the chemistry. The European Space Agency's JUICE spacecraft, launched in 2023, will also fly past Europa on its way to study Ganymede.

Neither spacecraft will land. But if they find the right ingredients, a future lander might one day melt or drill its way down. Scientists already practise by drilling through the ice of [[@antarctica|Antarctica]] to reach the hidden lakes beneath.

text: The mimic octopus pretends to be other animals by changing three things at once: its colour, its shape and the way it moves. In seconds, its brown skin can flash into bold brown-and-white stripes. Then it arranges its arms and body to look like a dangerous animal.

Its best-known acts are a venomous lionfish, a flat sole fish skimming over the sand and a poisonous banded sea snake. [[predator|Predators]] that have learned to avoid those animals think twice. Many animals can [[@camouflage|camouflage]] themselves to blend in. The mimic octopus does the opposite. It stands out, while dressed as something you shouldn't eat.

st.prompt: To copy a lionfish, what does the mimic octopus do?

options.t: Spreads its arms wide around its body like spiky fins
Grows sharp spines on its skin
Turns completely invisible

st.reveal: Lionfish have long, venomous fin spines. The octopus fans out its striped arms around it as it hovers, so it looks like a lionfish drifting through the water. Predators that know to avoid lionfish leave it alone.

src: Norman M.D., Finn J. and Tregenza T. (2001) Dynamic mimicry in an Indo-Malayan octopus. Proceedings of the Royal Society B.
Smithsonian Ocean, Octopuses.
n.certNote: The mimic octopus's main disguises, such as the lionfish, flatfish and sea snake, are well recorded on video. Some other claimed disguises, such as jellyfish or mantis shrimp, rest on fewer sightings, and scientists are still studying whether the octopus chooses each disguise on purpose.

d.try: Play mimic octopus. With a friend, choose three animals and agree on a body shape for each using only your arms, like flat and wide for a flatfish. Take turns acting them out silently while the other guesses. Then try changing between them as fast as you can.
myth: The mimic octopus copies other animals by changing its body into theirs.

It doesn't grow new parts. It uses colour changes, body shape, the way it holds its arms and the way it swims. It's like a very good actor using costume, posture and movement rather than becoming someone else.
facts: muddy and sandy seabeds in the warm Indo-Pacific, often near river mouths

sec.t:
Divers had glimpsed this octopus for years, but scientists first recorded it properly in 1998, at the mouth of a river in Sulawesi, Indonesia. They were astonished. Other octopuses copy the colour of rocks and seaweed. This one copied animals.

It got its scientific name, *Thaumoctopus mimicus*, in 2005. *Thauma* means "wonder" in Greek.

As a flatfish, the octopus pulls its arms together behind it and flattens its body into a leaf shape. It then swims fast just above the sand, rippling like a sole. Some soles in these waters are poisonous to eat, so a hungry fish has good reason to leave it alone.

As a lionfish, it spreads its striped arms all around its body like long, spiky fins. As a sea snake, it hides most of its body in a hole and stretches out two banded arms in opposite directions. With its head hidden, they look like the black-and-white bands of a [[@sea-snakes|sea snake]].

Some divers say they have also seen it imitate jellyfish, stingrays or mantis shrimp. These are harder to prove.

{{story:octopus-colour}}

An octopus's skin is packed with thousands of tiny colour sacs called chromatophores. Each one holds yellow, red, brown or black [[pigment|pigment]]. Muscles around each sac stretch it open or squeeze it shut. The octopus's brain controls them directly, so patterns can change in less than a second.

Below the colour sacs are cells that reflect light and make shimmering whites and blues. Together they work like a living screen with millions of [[pixel|pixels]], the same system that lets [[@octopus-colour|octopuses change colour]] to match rocks and weed.

The most puzzling part is that the octopus seems to pick its disguise to suit the threat. Researchers watched one hide as a sea snake when damselfish pestered it. Banded sea snakes eat damselfish, so that disguise would scare them most.

Octopuses have about 500 million nerve cells, roughly as many as the thinking layer of a dog's brain. Two-thirds of them are in the arms, not the head. That might help each arm play its part in a disguise. Scientists still argue about how much the octopus plans its acts and how much is instinct. Either way, it shows how [[@octopus-smart|clever octopuses]] can be.

Mimic octopuses live on flat, muddy or sandy seabeds in the warm waters around Indonesia, the [[@world-philippines|Philippines]], northern Australia and nearby seas. There is nowhere to hide, no coral and no rocks. Pretending to be something dangerous may be the best defence on such open ground.

They hunt small fish, crabs and worms, often poking their arms into burrows. When they are not acting, they look plain and brownish, almost boring. The stripes appear only when they move into the open. Like other octopuses, they have three hearts and blue blood.

A close cousin, the wonderpus, lives in the same areas and also has bold stripes. Copying another animal's warning colours isn't rare in nature, and some of the best tricks on land belong to the colour-changing [[@power-chameleon|chameleon]].

text: A [[tsunami|tsunami]] warning starts with an earthquake. Seismometers, instruments that feel the ground shaking, pick up a big quake under the sea within a minute or two. Computers work out where it struck and how strong it was.

If the quake is big and shallow enough to lift the sea floor, warning centres send an alert. [[sensor|Sensors]] on the sea floor and tide gauges along the coast then check whether a wave is really on its way and how large it is.
The warning goes out by text message, radio, TV, sirens and loudspeakers. People along the coast are told to move to high ground before the waves arrive.

st.prompt: You are on a beach and the sea suddenly drains away, leaving fish flapping on the sand. What should you do?

options.t: Move quickly inland or to high ground
Walk out to look at the sea floor
Wait for the water to come back slowly

st.reveal: A sea that pulls back fast can mean a tsunami is a few minutes away. The water can return as a wall of fast-moving sea. Head inland or uphill straight away and stay there until officials say it is safe.

myth: A tsunami is one giant wave that curls over like a surfing wave.
A tsunami is usually a series of waves, often arriving minutes apart, and the first is not always the biggest. Near shore it often looks like a fast, rising flood rather than a curling breaker.

sec.h: Why there is time to warn
sec.t:
A [[@tsunami|tsunami]] is a series of waves made when a large patch of sea floor jerks up or down, usually in an [[@earthquakes|earthquake]]. The whole depth of the ocean moves, not just the surface.

In deep water these waves are fast, about 800 km/h, but only about a metre high. Ships hardly feel them. As they reach shallow water near shore, they slow down and pile up, sometimes into walls of water many metres tall.

Earthquake signals travel through rock in seconds or minutes, far faster than the waves. A coast hundreds of kilometres away may have an hour or more. A coast right next to the quake may have only minutes, so people there are taught to move as soon as they feel a strong shake.

On 26 December 2004, a huge earthquake struck under the sea off Sumatra, in Indonesia. It set off a tsunami that crossed the Indian Ocean and killed about 230,000 people in 14 countries. In India, the coasts of Tamil Nadu and the [[@andaman|Andaman and Nicobar Islands]] were badly hit.

At the time, the Pacific Ocean had a warning system, started in Hawaii in 1949. The Indian Ocean had none.

On a beach in Phuket, Thailand, a ten-year-old British girl named Tilly Smith saw the sea froth and draw back. She had learned about tsunamis at school just two weeks before. She told her parents, who warned others, and the beach was cleared before the waves arrived.

After 2004, countries around the Indian Ocean built a warning system together. India's part is the Indian Tsunami Early Warning Centre at INCOIS in Hyderabad, which began work in 2007.

It watches for earthquakes around the clock using seismic stations, sea-floor pressure sensors and tide gauges. It aims to send an alert within about ten minutes of a big undersea quake. It also warns other countries around the Indian Ocean.

Warnings only work if people act on them. So coastal towns hold drills, put up evacuation signs and mark safe routes uphill. Many coastal villages in Odisha and Tamil Nadu now practise what to do. Schoolchildren learn the signs Tilly Smith knew: a strong earthquake, a sudden roar, or the sea rushing away from the shore.

text: When you fall, [[gravity|gravity]] pulls you down and you speed up. But as you go faster, you crash into more and more air [[molecule|molecules]] every second. The air pushes back. This push is called air resistance, or [[drag|drag]].

A falling skydiver with arms and legs spread soon reaches a speed where the drag pushing up equals the pull of gravity. They stop speeding up. This top speed, about 200 km/h belly-first, is called terminal [[velocity|velocity]].

A parachute is a big [[canopy|canopy]] of light, strong cloth. When it opens, it catches a huge amount of air, so the drag becomes far stronger. The skydiver slows sharply until a new, much gentler top speed is reached, slow enough to land safely on their feet.

options.t: It collapsed and he used his spare at once
It worked and gave a smooth ride

st.reveal: Adrian Nicholas said the pyramid of wood and canvas gave a smoother ride than modern parachutes. Because it was so heavy, he cut himself free and landed with a modern parachute, to avoid being crushed by it on the ground.

myth: Heavy things always fall faster than light things.

Without air, a hammer and a feather fall at the same speed, as an astronaut showed on the Moon in 1971. On Earth, air resistance slows light, spread-out things much more than heavy, compact ones. A parachute uses this to slow a person down.

sec.t:
Drag depends on how big you are from the front and how fast you're moving. A pebble and a sheet of paper weigh about the same, but the paper drifts slowly down because it's wide and flat. Crumple the paper into a ball, and it drops like the pebble.

A parachute might be as wide as a classroom. Spread out, it pushes against so much air that a person under it falls at only around 15 to 20 km/h. Many parachutes have a small hole at the top. This lets some air escape steadily, so the canopy doesn't swing wildly from side to side. Nature uses the same idea: dandelion [[@seeds-fly|seeds]] float on tiny parachutes of fluffy threads.

Around 1485, the Italian artist and inventor [[@leonardo|Leonardo da Vinci]] sketched a parachute in his notebook. It was a pyramid of linen stretched over a wooden frame. He wrote that a person could jump from any height with it and not be hurt.

For more than 500 years, nobody knew if it would work. In 2000, a British skydiver, Adrian Nicholas, built one from wood, canvas and rope and jumped with it from a hot-air balloon over South Africa. It worked, giving a smooth ride. Because it weighed so much, he cut it loose partway down and used a modern parachute to land.

One of the first parachute jumps from a balloon came in 1797, when André-Jacques Garnerin dropped above Paris under a silk canopy.

{{story:seeds-fly}}

Parachutes can work wherever there's air. In 2021, NASA's [[@tech-robots-space|Perseverance rover]] landed on Mars with the help of a parachute about 21.5 metres wide. Mars has very thin air, so the parachute alone couldn't slow it enough, and rockets did the last part. Engineers hid a secret message in the parachute's pattern of red and white panels, written in a computer code.

India's [[@gaganyaan|Gaganyaan]] programme will use parachutes too. When the crew capsule comes back from space, a set of parachutes will open one after another to slow it down for a splashdown in the sea. [[@india-space-budget|ISRO]] has tested them by dropping a dummy capsule from a helicopter.

Old round parachutes simply drifted wherever the wind blew. Most modern sport parachutes are rectangles that work like a wing. Skydivers pull on handles connected to the back edges to turn left or right, and pull both together to slow down just before landing.

Every skydiver carries a spare parachute, and many carry a small device that opens it automatically if they fall too low too fast. With good training, skydiving is a carefully managed sport.

text: Steel is made by turning iron ore, a reddish rock, into iron, then carefully controlling how much carbon is left in it. Pure iron is fairly soft. Iron with a lot of carbon is hard but snaps easily. Steel sits in between, with just a little carbon, usually less than 2%. That makes it strong and tough at the same time.

Most steel is made in one of two ways. Giant blast furnaces melt iron ore with coke, a form of coal, and the molten iron is then cleaned up into steel. Electric furnaces melt old scrap steel and make it new. Either way, the liquid steel is poured, cooled and rolled into sheets, bars, beams and wires. Most steel is magnetic, unlike aluminium or copper, so recycling plants can pull it out of mixed scrap with giant magnets.

st.prompt: To turn iron into steel, steelmakers mostly control the amount of one other element. Which?

options.t: Carbon
Gold
Oxygen

st.reveal: Iron from a blast furnace has too much carbon, which makes it brittle. Steelmakers blow oxygen through it to burn off most of the carbon, leaving just a little. Getting that small amount right is what makes steel strong.

myth: Stainless steel can never rust.
Stainless steel resists rust because chromium forms an invisible protective skin. Salty water, scratches or harsh cleaners can break that skin, and then even stainless steel can get rust spots.

sec.t:
Iron ore is iron joined to oxygen, a lot like [[@rust|rust]]. To free the iron, steelworks pour ore, coke and limestone into the top of a blast furnace, a tower as tall as a 10-storey building. Hot air is blasted in at the bottom.

The coke burns, reaching about 1,500 °C, and takes the oxygen away from the ore. Liquid iron trickles to the bottom. The limestone grabs sand and other unwanted bits, forming a crust called slag that floats on top. Workers tap the furnace and the glowing iron flows out like orange syrup.

People started using iron more than 3,000 years ago, at the start of the [[@iron-age|Iron Age]]. Smiths in South India made a famous high-carbon steel called wootz, which was traded far to the west and used for strong, patterned blades.

Ancient Indian metalworkers were skilled with iron too. In Delhi, an iron pillar about 7 metres tall has stood for around 1,600 years with very little rust. It is wrought iron, not steel. Scientists think a thin protective layer, helped by phosphorus in the iron and Delhi's fairly dry air, has kept it safe.

Cheap steel arrived in 1856, when Henry Bessemer in England found a way to blow air through molten iron to burn off carbon quickly. Suddenly steel could be made by the tonne, and it powered the later [[@industrial-revolution|Industrial Revolution]]: railways, ships and bridges. In 1907 Jamsetji Tata's dream became Tata Steel at Jamshedpur, India's first large steel works, which produced its first steel in 1912.

The world makes about 1.85 billion tonnes of steel a year. China makes about half. India comes second and is growing fast. The frames of [[@skyscrapers|skyscrapers]], the bars inside concrete, cars, ships, washing machines and nails are all steel.

Making steel from ore gives off a lot of [[carbon-dioxide|carbon dioxide]], around 7 to 9% of the world's total by many estimates. Recycling scrap in electric furnaces produces far less, and steel can be recycled again and again without losing strength. Some companies are now testing steel made with hydrogen instead of coal, which gives off water vapour instead of carbon dioxide.

text: गायक-मंडली, जिसे अंग्रेज़ी में क्वायर कहते हैं, ऐसे लोगों का समूह है जो साथ मिलकर गाते हैं। एक आवाज़ जैसी आवाज़ निकालने के लिए वे अलग-अलग हिस्सों में बँटते हैं, एक संचालक के इशारों पर चलते हैं, एक ही पल में साँस लेते हैं और हर समय एक-दूसरे को सुनते रहते हैं। हर गायक आसपास के लोगों से घुलने-मिलने के लिए अपना [[pitch|सुर]], अपनी आवाज़ की तेज़ी और अपना समय ठीक करता रहता है।

ज़्यादातर गायक-मंडलियों में चार मुख्य हिस्से होते हैं: सबसे ऊँचा सोप्रानो, फिर ऑल्टो, टेनर और बेस। जब ये हिस्से एक ही समय पर अलग-अलग सुर गाते हैं, तो हार्मनी बनती है, यानी सुरों का मेल। यह भरी-पूरी, परतों वाली आवाज़ कोई अकेली [[@voice|आवाज़]] अपने दम पर नहीं निकाल सकती।

sec.t:
सोप्रानो अक्सर वह धुन गाते हैं जिसे तुम गुनगुनाओगे। ऑल्टो थोड़ा नीचे गाते हैं और बीच की जगह भरते हैं। टेनर पुरुषों की आवाज़ों में ऊँचे होते हैं, और बेस वे नीचे वाले सुर देते हैं जो संगीत को थामे रखते हैं, जैसे किसी इमारत की नींव।

बच्चों की मंडलियाँ अक्सर बस दो या तीन हिस्सों में गाती हैं, क्योंकि छोटी उम्र में आवाज़ें अभी ऊँची और नीची में नहीं बँटी होतीं। कुछ मंडलियाँ एक स्वर में गाती हैं, सब एक ही सुर पर। यह आसान लगता है, पर इसे बिल्कुल एक साथ, एकदम सही गाना मुश्किल है। "फ़्रेर ज़ाक" जैसा राउंड हार्मनी शुरू करने का बढ़िया तरीका है, क्योंकि सब एक ही धुन गाते हैं पर अलग-अलग समय पर शुरू करते हैं।

असली राज़ है सुनना। हर गायक को एक साथ अपनी आवाज़ भी सुननी होती है और बगल वालों की भी। अगर कोई सुर ज़रा नीचे लग रहा है, तो वह उसे थोड़ा ऊपर खिसकाता है। अगर उसकी आवाज़ पड़ोसियों से ज़्यादा तेज़ है, तो वह थोड़ा धीमा कर लेता है।

2013 में स्वीडन की गोथेनबर्ग यूनिवर्सिटी के शोधकर्ताओं ने गायक-मंडली के अभ्यास के दौरान गायकों की धड़कनें नापीं। जब मंडली साथ में धीमी, शांत पंक्तियाँ गा रही थी, तो गायकों की धड़कनें साथ-साथ बढ़ती और घटती दिखीं। इसकी वजह शायद एक जैसी, साझा साँस है। बहुत-से लोग कहते हैं कि समूह में गाने से उन्हें सुकून मिलता है और वे दूसरों से ज़्यादा जुड़ा हुआ महसूस करते हैं।

ऑस्ट्रिया की वियना बॉयज़ क्वायर 1498 में शुरू हुई और आज भी दुनिया भर में घूमती है। ब्रिटेन में बड़े गिरजाघरों की मंडलियाँ सदियों से रोज़ की प्रार्थना सभाओं में गाती आई हैं। अमेरिका में अफ़्रीकी-अमेरिकी गिरजाघरों की गॉस्पेल मंडलियाँ तालियों, झूमने और दमदार अकेली आवाज़ों के साथ गाती हैं।

भारत की अपनी सामूहिक गायन परंपराएँ हैं। भजन और कीर्तन मंडलियाँ भक्ति गीत गाती हैं, जिनमें एक मुखिया पंक्ति गाता है और सब उसे दोहराते हैं। [[@qawwali|क़व्वाली]] में मुख्य गायक के पीछे एक कोरस होता है जो तालियाँ बजाता है और जवाब देता है। पूर्वोत्तर भारत में गिरजाघरों की मंडलियाँ मशहूर हैं, और 2010 में [[@shillong|शिलॉन्ग]] चैंबर क्वायर ने टीवी मुक़ाबला इंडियाज़ गॉट टैलेंट जीता।

गायक-मंडली में गाने के लिए सितारा होना ज़रूरी नहीं। बहुत-से स्कूलों, पूजा-स्थलों और सामुदायिक केंद्रों में ऐसी मंडलियाँ होती हैं जो नए लोगों का स्वागत करती हैं। मुखिया हिस्से सुनाकर या लिखे हुए संगीत से सिखाता है, और गायक किसी मज़बूत आवाज़ वाले के बगल में खड़े होकर सीखते हैं।

गायक-मंडली में गाना कुछ-कुछ [[@orchestra|ऑर्केस्ट्रा]] में बजाने जैसा है, फ़र्क बस इतना है कि साज़ तुम्हारे अंदर है। उसे नया ख़रीदा नहीं जा सकता, इसलिए मंडली के मुखिया गायकों को सिखाते हैं कि आवाज़ को आराम से गर्म करें और चिल्लाएँ नहीं। बहुत-से लोग अस्सी बरस की उम्र तक भी मंडलियों में गाते रहते हैं।

text: महाराष्ट्र के एलोरा का कैलास मंदिर एक पूरे आकार का हिंदू मंदिर है, जिसमें शिखर, मंडप, आँगन, पुल और खंभे हैं, और यह सब एक ही चट्टान से तराशा गया है। अलग-अलग पत्थरों से बनाने के बजाय 8वीं सदी के कारीगरों ने बेसाल्ट की एक पहाड़ी में गहरी खाइयाँ काटीं। उन्होंने बीच में एक विशाल खंड खड़ा छोड़ा और फिर उस खंड को अंदर-बाहर से तराशकर मंदिर बना दिया।
यह दुनिया के सबसे बड़े [[monolith|एकाश्म]] ढाँचों में से एक है। मंदिर शिव को समर्पित है, और इसे हिमालय में शिव के निवास, कैलास पर्वत, जैसा दिखने के लिए बनाया गया था।

sec.h: ऊपर से नीचे की ओर नक्काशी
sec.t:
ज़्यादातर इमारतें ज़मीन से ऊपर उठती हैं। कैलास मंदिर आसमान से नीचे उतरा। कारीगरों ने पहाड़ी की चोटी से शुरुआत की और चट्टान के एक खंड के चारों ओर तीन विशाल खाइयाँ काटीं, जिससे लगभग एक क्रिकेट मैदान जितना लंबा आँगन खुल गया।

फिर उन्होंने खंड को आकार दिया, शिखर के ऊपरी हिस्से से शुरू करके नीचे की ओर। इसका मतलब था कि काम करते हुए वे ऊँचे मचान बनाने के बजाय ख़ुद चट्टान पर खड़े रह सकते थे। कमरे और मंडप अंदर से खोखले किए गए। हर खंभा, हर सीढ़ी और हर खिड़की पहले से सोचनी पड़ी, क्योंकि गलती से हटाई गई चट्टान हमेशा के लिए चली जाती।

ज़्यादातर इतिहासकार इस मंदिर को राष्ट्रकूट [[dynasty|राजवंश]] के राजा कृष्ण प्रथम से जोड़ते हैं, जिन्होंने 700 के दशक (ईस्वी) में राज किया। काम में शायद कई साल और भारी संख्या में कारीगर लगे, और कुछ हिस्से शायद बाद के शासकों ने पूरे करवाए।

चट्टान हटाना सबसे बड़ा काम था। अनुमान है कि लोहे की छेनियों, हथौड़ों और कुदालों से लगभग 2 लाख टन पत्थर छीला गया। यह मोटे तौर पर 40,000 हाथियों के वज़न जितना है।

मंदिर नक्काशियों से भरा पड़ा है। असली आकार के पत्थर के हाथी मानो मुख्य चबूतरे को अपनी पीठ पर उठाए हुए हैं। आँगन में पत्थर के दो ऊँचे स्तंभ और पत्थर के दो हाथी खड़े हैं।

दीवारों पर [[@ramayana|रामायण]] और [[@mahabharata|महाभारत]] के दृश्य हैं और शिव-पार्वती की बहुत-सी मूर्तियाँ। एक मशहूर पट्टिका में राक्षसराज रावण कैलास पर्वत को हिलाने की कोशिश कर रहा है, और शिव शांति से पैर के एक अँगूठे से उसे दबाकर स्थिर रखे हुए हैं। रंग और पलस्तर के निशान बताते हैं कि मंदिर कभी रंगा हुआ था, शायद बर्फ़ से ढके पहाड़ की तरह सफ़ेद, हालाँकि ज़्यादातर रंग अब उड़ चुका है।

कैलास एलोरा की उसी चट्टान में काटी गई 34 गुफ़ाओं में से गुफ़ा 16 है। इनमें कुछ बौद्ध हैं, कुछ हिंदू और कुछ जैन, जो कई सदियों में अगल-बगल बनाई गईं। ये गुफ़ाएँ दिखाती हैं कि एक ही जगह अलग-अलग [[@religions-world|धर्म]] माने और सँभाले जाते थे।

1983 में एलोरा यूनेस्को विश्व धरोहर स्थल बना, उसी साल जब पास की अजंता गुफ़ाएँ, जो अपने [[@ajanta-colours|प्राचीन चित्रों]] के लिए मशहूर हैं। आज लोग आँगन में घूमते हुए उस मंदिर को ऊपर निहारते हैं जो कभी बनाया नहीं गया, बस खोदकर बाहर निकाला गया।

text: टेराकोटा का इतालवी में मतलब है "पकी हुई मिट्टी"। यह वह मिट्टी है जिसे आकार देकर [[kiln|भट्ठी]], यानी बेहद गर्म भट्टे, में तब तक पकाया जाता है जब तक वह सख़्त और लाल-भूरी न हो जाए। गमले और खपरैल भी इसी मिट्टी से बनते हैं। जब कलाकार इससे मूर्तियाँ, टाइलें या सजावटी चीज़ें बनाते हैं, तो उसे टेराकोटा कला कहते हैं।

इंसान हज़ारों साल से टेराकोटा बनाते आए हैं, क्योंकि मिट्टी सस्ती है और लगभग हर जगह मिलती है। इसे साँचे में दबाया, बेला, चुटकी से खींचा या तराशा जा सकता है। पकने के बाद यह बहुत लंबे समय तक टिकती है, ज़मीन में दबी रहे तब भी।
दुनिया की कुछ सबसे मशहूर कलाकृतियाँ टेराकोटा की हैं, सिंधु घाटी के शहरों की खिलौना गाड़ियों से लेकर चीन की [[@mystery-terracotta|ज़मीन में दबी पूरी सेना]] तक।

sec.t:
कच्ची मिट्टी इसलिए नरम होती है क्योंकि उसमें पानी भरा होता है। धूप में सूखकर वह कड़ी तो हो जाती है, पर भीगने पर फिर कीचड़ बन जाती है। पकाने से वह हमेशा के लिए बदल जाती है। लगभग 900 से 1,000 °C वाली भट्ठी में मिट्टी के नन्हे कण आपस में जुड़ जाते हैं।

ज़्यादातर मिट्टी में कुदरती रूप से लोहा होता है, और उसी से टेराकोटा को उसका गर्म लाल या नारंगी रंग मिलता है। यही रंग बहुत सी [[@bricks|ईंटों]] का भी है, जो असल में टेराकोटा के ही टुकड़े हैं।

बिना ग्लेज़ वाला टेराकोटा थोड़ा छिद्रदार रहता है, यानी उसमें नन्हे छेद होते हैं जिनसे पानी रिस सकता है। इसीलिए मिट्टी के *मटके* का पानी ठंडा रहता है। थोड़ा पानी रिसकर बाहर से [[evaporation|भाप बनकर उड़]] जाता है। ग्लेज़ वाला टेराकोटा, जिस पर काँच जैसी परत चढ़ी होती है, पानी रोक लेता है और चटक रंगों में भी आ सकता है।

दक्षिण एशिया का कुछ सबसे पुराना टेराकोटा [[@indus-cities|सिंधु घाटी के शहरों]] से आया है, जैसे हड़प्पा और मोहनजोदड़ो, 4,000 साल से भी पहले का। [[archaeologist|पुरातत्वविदों]] को वहाँ मिट्टी के जानवर, घूमने वाले पहियों वाली छोटी गाड़ियाँ, सीटियाँ, छोटी मूर्तियाँ और मुहरें मिली हैं।

इनमें से बहुत सी चीज़ें बिल्कुल खिलौनों जैसी लगती हैं। हड़प्पा की मिट्टी की बैलगाड़ी उन बैलगाड़ियों से बहुत अलग नहीं है जो आज भी भारत के गाँवों में दिखती हैं। वहाँ शुरू हुई [[@pottery|मिट्टी के बर्तनों]] की परंपरा बदलाव के साथ तब से चलती आई है।

पश्चिम बंगाल के विष्णुपुर में मल्ल राजाओं ने ज़्यादातर 17वीं और 18वीं सदी में लगभग पूरी तरह ईंट और टेराकोटा के मंदिर बनवाए। दीवारें मिट्टी की हज़ारों नक्काशीदार टाइलों से ढकी हैं, जिनमें रामायण और महाभारत के दृश्य, कृष्ण का जीवन, शिकार पर निकली टोलियाँ, सैनिक और जहाज़ दिखते हैं।

जोड़ बांग्ला मंदिर तो बंगाल के गाँव की झोंपड़ी की घुमावदार छप्पर वाली छत की मिट्टी में नकल करता है। पास के पाँचमुड़ा गाँव में कुम्हार आज भी लंबी गर्दन वाला बाँकुड़ा का घोड़ा बनाते हैं, जो अब भारतीय लोक शिल्प की पहचान बन चुका है।

तमिलनाडु में गाँव वाले रखवाले देवता अय्यनार का सम्मान विशाल टेराकोटा घोड़ों से करते हैं, जिनमें से कुछ इंसान से भी ऊँचे होते हैं और खेतों के किनारे रखे जाते हैं। ये टुकड़ों में बनाए जाते हैं, खुली आग में पकाए जाते हैं और वहीं जोड़े जाते हैं। सालों में बारिश और धूप इन्हें घिस देती है, और नए बनाए जाते हैं।

दुनिया भर में बाग़बानी करने वाले आज भी टेराकोटा के गमले इस्तेमाल करते हैं, क्योंकि उनमें जड़ें साँस ले पाती हैं। वही पकी मिट्टी अमेरिका के ओहायो की किसी खिड़की पर जेरेनियम का पौधा थामे है, और लखनऊ के किसी आँगन में तुलसी।

text: A cooperative, or co-op, is a business owned and run by the people who use it. Instead of investors owning it to earn a profit, the members own it together. They might be farmers selling milk, shoppers buying groceries, workers running a factory or neighbours sharing a bank.

Each member usually gets one vote, no matter how much money they have put in. Any surplus is either reinvested or shared among members, often according to how much each one used the co-op. A [[cooperative|cooperative]] lets ordinary people do together what none of them could afford to do alone.

st.reveal: The basic rule of cooperatives is one member, one vote. In an ordinary company, people who own more shares get more votes, so a rich investor can outvote many small ones.

sec.t:
In the 1840s, workers in the English mill town of Rochdale were poor and often cheated by shopkeepers. Flour was mixed with chalk, and scales were rigged. During the [[@industrial-revolution|Industrial Revolution]], many working families had no one to complain to.

So in 1844, a group of 28 men, many of them [[@knitting-weaving|weavers]], saved up and opened their own shop on Toad Lane. At first it sold only butter, sugar, flour, oatmeal and candles. They sold honest goods at fair weights, shared the profits among members, and gave each member one vote. Their rules became the model for cooperatives around the world.

In 1959, seven women living in a crowded building in Girgaum, Mumbai, wanted to earn a little money without leaving their homes. They borrowed ₹80 and began rolling [[@papad|papads]] on their terrace.

They set strict rules. Every papad had to taste the same. Every member was an owner, called a sister, and nobody was just an employee. The organisation, Shri Mahila Griha Udyog Lijjat Papad, grew branch by branch across India. Today it is run by tens of thousands of women, who still mostly roll papads at home and bring them to a centre each day.

In the USA, about one in three people belongs to a credit union, a bank owned by its customers. Cranberry farmers own Ocean Spray, and the news agency Associated Press is a cooperative of newspapers and broadcasters. Many rural American homes still get their electricity from co-ops formed in the 1930s, when private companies didn't think it was worth running wires to farms.

The International Cooperative Alliance says co-ops around the world have more than a billion members. The United Nations named 2012, and again 2025, the International Year of Cooperatives. Even Mumbai's [[@lunchbox-dabbawala|dabbawalas]] share their earnings as partners rather than as staff of a single boss.

text: A World Heritage Site is a place so important that it is treated as belonging to all of humanity, as well as to the country it sits in. It might be a building, like the [[@taj-mahal|Taj Mahal]], a ruined city, a forest or a whole mountain range.

The list is kept by UNESCO, the part of the United Nations that looks after education, science and culture. Countries suggest places, experts check them, and a committee decides each year which ones join.
There are now more than 1,200 sites in over 160 countries. India has more than 40 of them, and the United States has about 25.

The country where the site is keeps owning and looking after it. UNESCO keeps the list, gives advice and sometimes helps with money. If a country lets a site fall apart, UNESCO can warn it and, in the end, take the site off the list.

sec.t:
The idea grew out of a rescue. In the 1950s, Egypt decided to build the Aswan High Dam across the Nile. Its huge lake would flood ancient temples, including Abu Simbel, carved into a cliff more than 3,000 years ago.

UNESCO asked the world for help, and about 50 countries joined in. Between 1964 and 1968, engineers sliced Abu Simbel into large blocks, lifted them about 65 m up the hill, and fitted them back together. People realised that some places were too precious to leave to one country alone.

Sites are cultural, natural or mixed. Cultural sites are made by people, such as the ruins of [[@hampi|Hampi]] or Dholavira, one of the great [[@indus-cities|Indus cities]], added in 2021. Natural sites protect wild places, like Kaziranga, home of the [[@rhino-kaziranga|one-horned rhino]], or the [[@grand-canyon|Grand Canyon]].

A few sites are both. India's only mixed site is Khangchendzonga National Park in [[@sikkim|Sikkim]], which protects high mountains and also places sacred to the people who live there.

sec.h: How a place gets on the list
sec.t:
Getting listed takes years. A country first puts a place on a "tentative list" of hopefuls. Then it writes a long report, called a nomination, explaining why the place has "outstanding universal value", meaning it matters to people everywhere.

Experts visit and write their own reports. For cultural sites, this is a group called ICOMOS. For natural sites, it is the IUCN, a world nature organisation. Finally, the World Heritage Committee, made up of 21 countries, meets each summer and votes.

The place must also have a plan for its care: who guards it, how visitors are managed and what building is allowed nearby. In 2023, the temples of the [[@hoysalas|Hoysala kings]] in Karnataka and Santiniketan in West Bengal, where the poet Rabindranath [[@tagore|Tagore]] built his school, were both added after this long process.

sec.h: When a site is in trouble
sec.t:
Some sites are put on a "List of World Heritage in Danger" because of war, floods, pollution or too much building. That warning often brings help and money.

If things get worse, a site can be removed. Germany's Dresden Elbe Valley lost its place in 2009 after a large road bridge was built across it. In 2021, the waterfront of Liverpool in England was removed too. Being listed is an honour, and it comes with homework that never really ends.

text: The Oscars, officially the Academy Awards, are prizes for films. They are given each year by the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences, a group of more than 10,000 film professionals, such as actors, directors, editors and sound designers.

Members vote for the best work of the previous year in more than 20 categories, from Best Picture to Best Visual Effects. Winners receive a golden statuette of a knight holding a sword and standing on a reel of film. The ceremony is held in [[@los-angeles|Los Angeles]], usually in March, and the 98th took place in 2026.

sec.t:
Each branch of the Academy nominates in its own area. Editors pick the editing nominees, and cinematographers choose the cinematography ones. Then all voting members can choose winners in almost every category.

Best Picture uses a special system called a preferential ballot. Voters rank the films from favourite to least favourite. If no film gets more than half the first choices, the film with the fewest is knocked out and its votes go to each voter's next choice. This repeats until one film has a majority.

The statuette is about 34 centimetres tall and weighs about 3.9 kilograms, roughly as heavy as a newborn baby. It is made of metal and coated in 24-carat gold. Nobody is completely sure why it is called Oscar. One popular story says an Academy librarian thought it looked like her uncle Oscar, but this has never been proved.

During the Second World War, metal was scarce, so for a few years winners got statuettes made of painted plaster. They could swap them for metal ones after the war.

In 1983 costume designer Bhanu Athaiya became the first Indian to win an Oscar, for her work on the film *Gandhi*. In 1992 [[@satyajit-ray|Satyajit Ray]] received an honorary Oscar for his lifetime of films. He was very ill in a Kolkata hospital, so he accepted it by video.

In 2009 the British film *Slumdog Millionaire*, set in Mumbai, won eight Oscars. [[@ar-rahman|A.R. Rahman]] won two, for the music and for the song "Jai Ho", shared with lyricist Gulzar. Resul Pookutty won for sound mixing. In 2023 "Naatu Naatu" from the Telugu film *RRR* won Best Original Song, for composer M.M. Keeravani and lyricist Chandrabose. The same night, *The Elephant Whisperers*, about a couple in Tamil Nadu caring for an orphaned baby elephant, won Best Documentary Short.

Three films share the record of 11 Oscars: *Ben-Hur* (1959), *Titanic* (1997) and *The Lord of the Rings: The Return of the King* (2003). Walt Disney won more Oscars than any other person, mostly for cartoons.

The Oscars are often criticised too. For decades, few women and people of colour were nominated, and in 2015 and 2016 the online campaign #OscarsSoWhite drew attention to this. The Academy has since added thousands of new members from more countries. Many people also point out that the Oscars mostly reward English-language films, though the Korean film *Parasite* became the first non-English film to win Best Picture, in 2020.

text: Pelé and Diego Maradona were two of the greatest footballers ever. Pelé, from Brazil, won three [[@fifa-world-cup|World Cups]], in 1958, 1962 and 1970, the only player to do so. sec.h: Pelé: the boy with a sock ball
sec.t:
Edson Arantes do Nascimento was born in 1940 in Três Corações, Brazil, into a poor family. As a boy he played with a sock stuffed with newspaper or rags because his family could not afford a ball. Nobody is sure where his nickname "Pelé" came from.

He joined the club Santos at 15. At 17 he played in the 1958 World Cup in Sweden and scored twice in the final. He stayed at Santos for nearly 20 years. Late in his career he joined the New York Cosmos, helping to make football popular in the USA from a base in [[@new-york|New York]].

Diego Armando Maradona was born in 1960 in Lanús, near Buenos Aires, and grew up in a poor neighbourhood called Villa Fiorito. He was about 1.65 metres tall, but his balance and close control were astonishing. He seemed able to keep the ball no matter how many defenders surrounded him.

He played for Barcelona and then Napoli in Italy, where he led a struggling southern club to its first league titles in 1987 and 1990. In Naples he is still treated almost like a saint. [[mural|Murals]] of his face cover walls in the city, and Napoli's stadium was renamed after him when he died.

In the 1986 World Cup quarter-final, Argentina played England in Mexico City. Early in the second half, Maradona punched the ball into the net with his hand. The referee allowed it. Maradona later called it "the hand of God".

Four minutes later, he picked up the ball in his own half, dribbled past several England players and the goalkeeper, and scored. In 2002, a FIFA online poll voted it the Goal of the Century. Argentina went on to win the final against West Germany.

Maradona struggled with drug addiction. He was banned in 1991 and sent home from the 1994 World Cup after failing drug tests. He later coached Argentina, and died in 2020 at 60.

Pelé was named an athlete of the century by the International Olympic Committee and became Brazil's sports minister. In 2000 FIFA could not choose between them. An internet poll picked Maradona, a panel of experts picked Pelé, and they shared the award. Pelé died in 2022, aged 82. Both visited [[@kolkata|Kolkata]], where fans packed stadiums just to see them.

sec.t:
आवाज़ की लहरें कानों में जाकर सुनने वाली [[nerve|नसों]] में संकेत बन जाती हैं। दिमाग के सुनने वाले हिस्से सुर की ऊँचाई यानी [[pitch|पिच]], आवाज़ का ज़ोर और [[rhythm|लय]] पहचानते हैं। फिर ये संकेत आगे फैल जाते हैं।

हरकत की योजना बनाने वाले हिस्से ताल का अंदाज़ा लगाने लगते हैं, चाहे तुम चुपचाप बैठे हो। इसीलिए सिर हिलाने से ख़ुद को रोकना इतना मुश्किल होता है। दिमाग लगातार अंदाज़ा भी लगाता रहता है कि अगला सुर कौन-सा आएगा। जब गाना तुम्हें चौंकाता है, अचानक सुर बदलकर या मुखड़े से पहले ठहरकर, तो ये अंदाज़े टूट जाते हैं, और तुम्हें एक झटका-सा महसूस होता है।

यह बहुत जल्दी शुरू हो जाता है। कुछ ही महीने के शिशु साधारण बातचीत के मुकाबले साफ़ ताल वाले संगीत पर ज़्यादा कुलबुलाते और उछलते हैं। वैज्ञानिकों ने जिस भी इंसानी संस्कृति को देखा, वहाँ संगीत मिला, असम के गाँवों की लोरियों से लेकर अमेरिका के दक्षिण के मेहनत वाले गीतों तक। बहुत-से शोधकर्ता मानते हैं कि हमारा दिमाग जन्म से ही इसके लिए सधा हुआ है।

परिवार की किसी शादी या स्कूल ट्रिप का कोई गाना सुनो, और तुम सीधे उसी दिन में पहुँच सकते हो। संगीत और याददाश्त आपस में कसकर जुड़े हैं, कुछ इसलिए कि संगीत [[@emotions|भावनाएँ]] जगाता है, और भावुक पल याद रखना आसान होता है।

यह जुड़ाव इतना मज़बूत है कि अल्ज़ाइमर के मरीज़ों की भी मदद कर सकता है, जिस बीमारी में याददाश्त को नुकसान पहुँचता है। कुछ मरीज़ जो अपने रिश्तेदारों को पहचानने में भी अटकते हैं, अपनी जवानी के गानों का हर शब्द गा लेते हैं। भारत और अमेरिका समेत कई देशों के देखभाल-घरों में वहाँ रहने वालों को शांत करने और सुकून देने के लिए संगीत का इस्तेमाल होता है।

म्यूज़िक थेरेपिस्ट लोगों को ठीक होने में मदद के लिए गानों और लय का इस्तेमाल करते हैं। स्ट्रोक के बाद कुछ मरीज़ बोल नहीं पाते, पर गा सकते हैं। थेरेपिस्ट गाने के सहारे धीरे-धीरे उनकी बोली फिर से गढ़ते हैं।

एक-सी ताल पार्किंसन के मरीज़ों की भी मदद करती है, जिस बीमारी में चलना मुश्किल हो जाता है। किसी [[@rhythm-beat|ताल]] पर कदम मिलाकर चलने से उनके कदम ज़्यादा सधे हुए हो सकते हैं। कुछ अस्पतालों में समय से पहले जन्मे शिशुओं को भी हल्का संगीत या लोरियाँ सुनाई जाती हैं, जिससे शायद उन्हें सुकून मिलता है।

1993 में एक छोटी जाँच ने बताया कि मोत्सार्ट सुनने के बाद कॉलेज छात्रों ने कागज़ मोड़ने वाली एक पहेली में थोड़ा बेहतर किया। यह सुधार बस लगभग 10 से 15 मिनट टिका। फिर भी अख़बारों ने इसे "मोत्सार्ट इफ़ेक्ट" कह दिया। खिलौना कंपनियों ने शिशुओं के लिए मोत्सार्ट की सीडी बेचीं, और 1998 में अमेरिका के जॉर्जिया राज्य के गवर्नर ने तो हर नवजात को एक सीडी देने का प्रस्ताव भी रख दिया।

बाद की खोज में पता चला कि यह असर बहुत छोटा और थोड़ी देर का था, और शायद बस अच्छे मूड की निशानी था। कोई वाद्य बजाना सीखना अलग बात है। इससे सुनने, ध्यान लगाने और उँगलियों पर बारीक काबू की ट्रेनिंग होती है, और संगीतकारों के दिमाग में बाकी लोगों से कुछ फ़र्क दिखते हैं। वैज्ञानिक अब भी बहस कर रहे हैं कि इससे बच्चे दूसरे विषयों में बेहतर होते हैं या नहीं।

text: Metro trains keep time because they run on their own tracks, with no cars, cows or traffic lights to get in the way, and because computers watch every train all the time. The system knows exactly where each train is, how fast it's going and how far it is from the one ahead.

The tightest part of the timetable is not the journey between stations. It's the few seconds a train spends at each platform, letting people off and on. Engineers plan stations, doors and even floor markings to keep those stops short. Get them right and a line can send a train every two or three minutes at rush hour.

sec.t:
The very first underground railway opened in London in 1863. Its trains were pulled by steam engines, and passengers complained about the smoke. Electric trains took over in the 1890s and 1900s. New York's subway followed in 1904.

India's first metro opened in [[@kolkata|Kolkata]] in 1984, running under the city's crowded streets. The Delhi Metro started in 2002 and grew quickly. By 2025, Indian cities together had around 1,000 km of metro lines, one of the largest networks in the world, with more being built in cities from Pune to Patna.

A station stop might last only 20 or 30 seconds. If crowds hold the doors or squeeze in late, a train leaves a little behind time. The train behind it then catches up, and the delay can ripple down the whole line.

So metros fight for every second. Wide doors and wide platforms help people move quickly. Painted arrows show where to stand so people getting off aren't blocked. Many stations, especially newer ones, have glass walls and doors along the platform edge that line up exactly with the train doors. They keep people off the track and speed up boarding. Some metros also run extra trains on festival days or during big cricket matches, when stations suddenly fill.

In December 2020, part of the Delhi Metro's Magenta Line began running trains with no driver in the cab, a first in India. Computers start, stop and open the doors. Staff in a control room watch over everything and can step in.

Driverless metros already run in cities such as [[@dubai|Dubai]], Singapore and Copenhagen. They can run trains closer together and adjust quickly to crowds, the way a good [[@algorithms|algorithm]] adjusts to new information. A metro is a moving piece of [[@urban-planning|urban planning]] too. Where a line goes decides where shops, offices and homes will grow for decades.

text: The Ottomans were a [[dynasty|dynasty]] of Turkish rulers who built one of the largest and longest-lasting [[empire|empires]] in history. It began around 1299 with a chief called Osman, whose small territory lay in north-western Anatolia, today's Turkey. The name "Ottoman" comes from his name.

In 1453 the Ottomans captured Constantinople and made it their capital, Istanbul. At their height in the 1500s and 1600s, they ruled south-eastern Europe, Turkey, most of the Middle East including Mecca and Medina, and North Africa. The empire slowly weakened, sided with Germany in the First World War, and ended in 1922. The Republic of Turkey took its place.

myth: The Ottoman Empire was the same thing as modern Turkey.

Turkey grew out of the Ottoman heartland, but the empire was far bigger and more mixed. It included Greeks, Arabs, Armenians, Kurds, Jews, Serbs, Bulgarians and many others, speaking dozens of languages.

sec.t:
For a thousand years, Constantinople, the capital of the [[@byzantium|Byzantine Empire]], had resisted attackers. In 1453 the 21-year-old Sultan Mehmed II besieged it with a large army and some of the biggest cannons ever made, built by a Hungarian engineer named Orban.

The Byzantines had stretched a chain across their harbour, the Golden Horn. Mehmed had dozens of ships dragged over a hill on greased logs and launched them behind the chain. After almost two months, on 29 May 1453, his troops broke through the walls. Mehmed rebuilt the damaged city, invited people of many faiths to settle there and turned Hagia Sophia into a mosque.

The Ottoman Empire was a patchwork of peoples and religions. Muslims, Christians and Jews lived side by side. Under what is often called the millet system, religious communities ran many of their own affairs, such as marriage and schools, under their own leaders.

When Spain expelled its Jews in 1492, many found refuge in Ottoman cities. Ottoman cities were also places of trade and new habits. Coffee houses spread in Istanbul in the 1500s, and [[@coffee|coffee]] drinking later travelled to Europe. The empire also had links with India. In 1538 an Ottoman fleet sailed to help the Sultan of Gujarat fight the Portuguese at Diu.

From the late 1600s the empire began to lose ground. After a second failed siege of Vienna in 1683, European powers pushed it back. In the 1800s, nations such as Greece, Serbia and Bulgaria won independence, and Europeans began calling the empire "the sick man of Europe". Sultans tried reforms, building railways, schools and a new army.

The Ottomans joined the [[@world-war-one|First World War]] on Germany's side. During the war, the Ottoman government deported Armenians from their homes, and huge numbers died in massacres and forced marches. Estimates range from about 600,000 to 1.5 million people. Most historians, and many countries, call this the Armenian genocide. The government of Turkey disputes that word, though it accepts that many Armenians died.

After defeat in 1918, the empire was carved up by the winners. In India, many Muslims, supported by [[@gandhi|Gandhi]], joined the Khilafat movement, which campaigned to protect the Ottoman sultan's role as caliph, a religious leader for many Sunni Muslims.

In Turkey, an army officer named Mustafa Kemal, later called Atatürk, led a war of independence. The sultanate was abolished in 1922, the Republic of Turkey was declared in 1923, and the caliphate was abolished in 1924. Topkapı Palace, where sultans lived for centuries, is now a museum overlooking the Bosporus.

text: In the 1860s, getting from the east coast of the United States to California meant [[@usa-oregon-trail|months by wagon]] or by ship. So the government paid two companies to build a railroad across the continent. The Central Pacific started in Sacramento, California, and built east. The Union Pacific started near Omaha, Nebraska, and built west.

After six years of hard work, the two lines met at Promontory Summit in Utah on 10 May 1869. Now people and goods could cross the country by train in about a week. It changed America, though at a great cost to the people who built it and to the [[@native-nations|Native nations]] whose lands it crossed.

myth: The railroad was built mostly by machines.
It was built mostly by hand. Workers used picks, shovels, hammers, wheelbarrows, horses and explosives. Laying track meant carrying heavy iron rails and hammering spikes, one at a time.

sec.t:
Even while the Civil War was raging, President [[@abraham-lincoln|Abraham Lincoln]] signed the Pacific Railway Act in 1862. The government gave the companies loans and huge strips of land beside the track, which they could sell. The more track they laid, the more they earned, so each company rushed to lay as much as possible.

Since the [[@gold-rush|Gold Rush]], California had grown fast, but it was cut off from the rest of the country by deserts and mountains. A railroad would tie it to the East.

The Central Pacific could not find enough workers. So in 1865 it began hiring Chinese immigrants, many from Guangdong in southern China. Doubters thought they were too small for the work. They were wrong. At the peak, as many as 10,000 to 15,000 Chinese workers made up most of the Central Pacific's labour force.

They were paid less than white workers and often given the most dangerous jobs. Many died, though nobody kept a careful count. In 1867, thousands went on strike for better pay and shorter hours. The company cut off their food, and the strike ended after about a week, but it showed how much the railroad depended on them.

The Union Pacific had flatter ground but its own problems. Its workers were largely Irish immigrants, Civil War veterans, and freed African Americans. Its lines crossed the hunting grounds of the Lakota, Cheyenne and other nations, who fought back against the invasion of their land.

The railroads also carried hunters who shot millions of [[@bison-return|bison]], the animals many Plains nations depended on. Within about 20 years, the great herds were nearly gone.

On 10 May 1869, crowds gathered at Promontory Summit. A golden spike was tapped into place, and a [[telegraph|telegraph]] message, DONE, flashed across the country. In a famous photograph, workers from both lines shake hands. Chinese workers are almost absent from it.

In 2019, for the 150th anniversary, [[descendant|descendants]] of Chinese railroad workers gathered at the same spot to recreate the photo, this time with their ancestors' story included. In India, the first passenger train had run from Bombay to Thane in 1853, a journey of 34 km. America's new track was more than 80 times longer.

text: Rome has been called the Eternal City since ancient times. The Roman poet Tibullus used the phrase in the first century BCE, and Romans came to believe their city would last forever. In a way, it has. Rome was the centre of a great [[empire|empire]], then the centre of the Catholic Church, and today it is the capital of Italy.

Walk through Rome and you see every age at once. A 2,000-year-old temple stands beside a café. Ancient columns poke out of modern buildings. About 2.8 million people live in the city today, among ruins older than most countries.

st.prompt: The Pantheon's giant dome has stood for about 1,900 years. What is it made of?

options.t: Concrete, with no steel inside
Solid marble blocks
Bricks held together with iron bars

st.reveal: Roman builders used concrete made with lime and volcanic ash. They made it heavier at the bottom of the dome and lighter at the top, mixing in light volcanic stone. Modern concrete domes need steel rods inside. The Pantheon has none.

n.certNote: Legend says Rome was founded by Romulus in 753 BCE. Archaeologists have found huts on the Palatine Hill from around that time and earlier, so the legend's date is roughly right, but the story of Romulus and Remus is a myth.

myth: The emperor Nero played the fiddle while Rome burned in 64 CE.

The fiddle had not been invented yet. The Roman historian Tacitus wrote that Nero was away in the town of Antium when the fire started and came back to help organise relief. The story of him singing during the fire was a rumour even then.

sec.t:
Legend says twin boys, Romulus and Remus, were left beside the River Tiber and fed by a she-wolf. Romulus founded Rome on 21 April 753 BCE, and Romans still celebrate the city's birthday on that date. [[archaeologist|Archaeologists]] have found the remains of huts on the Palatine Hill from around that time and even earlier.

Rome grew across seven hills beside the Tiber. Over centuries, it became the capital of an [[@ancient-rome|empire]] that stretched from Britain to Egypt. Roads paved with stone linked it all, which is where the saying "all roads lead to Rome" comes from.

The ancient Romans built [[aqueduct|aqueducts]], channels that carried fresh water downhill from springs many kilometres away. The Aqua Virgo, finished in 19 BCE, still carries water to Rome today. It feeds the Trevi Fountain, finished in 1762.

Visitors throw coins over their shoulders into the fountain, because tradition says it means you will return to Rome. More than a million euros are collected each year, and the money goes to a charity that helps people in need.

Inside Rome lies [[@vatican|Vatican]] City, [[@extreme-smallest-countries|the smallest country in the world]], only about 0.44 km². It is the home of the Pope, the leader of the Catholic Church. St Peter's Basilica, one of the largest churches in the world, rises over a huge square.

In the nearby Sistine Chapel, [[@michelangelo|Michelangelo]] painted the ceiling between 1508 and 1512, mostly standing on scaffolding with his head tilted back. He also designed the great dome of St Peter's.

Because people have lived in Rome for so long, the city stands on layers of its own past. When builders dig a new metro line, they often find ancient houses, streets or burial places. Work can stop for months while archaeologists study them. One new station even displays objects found during digging, so travellers can see Rome's history on their way to work.

Roman influence spreads far beyond the city. [[@roman-numerals|Roman numerals]] still appear on clocks and in film credits, [[@latin-roots|Latin words]] fill English, and many legal ideas began in Roman law.

text: Grammar is the set of patterns a language uses to show how words fit together. Without it, you'd have a pile of words but no way to say who did what to whom, when it happened, or whether you are asking or telling.

Every human language has grammar, including sign languages and languages that have never been written down. It isn't a list of rules invented by teachers. Speakers follow most of it without thinking, and children pick it up long before they go to school.
Languages do the job in different ways. Some rely on word order, some on word endings, and some on small helper words.

st.prompt: Which word order is the most common among the world's languages?

options.t: Subject, object, verb, as in Hindi
Subject, verb, object, as in English
Verb, subject, object, as in Welsh

st.reveal: In a large survey of world languages, subject-object-verb came first, with subject-verb-object a close second. Orders that start with the verb, like Welsh, are much rarer.

n.certNote: Everyone agrees that all languages have grammar. Linguists still debate how much of it is built into the human brain and how much children learn from what they hear.

myth: Some languages have no grammar.

sec.t:
In English, word order carries much of the meaning. "The cat chased the mouse" and "The mouse chased the cat" use exactly the same words, but the order tells you who is running away. English usually goes subject, verb, object.

[[@hindi-language|Hindi]] often puts the verb at the end and uses small helper words to mark roles: *Billi ne chuhe ko pakda*, "The cat caught the mouse". *Ne* marks who did it and *ko* marks who it happened to, so the words can sometimes shuffle without confusion. Tamil and Japanese also put the verb last. In fact, subject, object, verb is the most common order among the world's languages, with English's order a close second.

Other languages pack information into the ends of words. In [[@sanskrit|Sanskrit]], nouns change their endings depending on their job in a sentence, so the word order is very free. Panini's *Ashtadhyayi*, written over 2,000 years ago, described these patterns in about 4,000 compact rules.

Many languages sort nouns into groups called genders. In Hindi, a book (*kitab*) is feminine and a room (*kamra*) is masculine, and that changes the words around them: *kitab achchhi hai*, but *kamra achchha hai*. Bengali, Turkish and Finnish have no gender for nouns at all. English has mostly lost the genders that Old English once had, keeping only he, she and it.

Children everywhere learn grammar at about the same pace, without lessons. A three-year-old who says "I goed" instead of "I went" isn't copying anyone. They have worked out the rule "add -ed for the past" and applied it a little too well.

In the 1950s and 1960s, the American linguist Noam Chomsky argued that humans are born with a "universal grammar", a kind of built-in blueprint for language. Others argue that children are simply excellent pattern-spotters who learn grammar from the speech around them. The debate is still going.

One striking clue came from Nicaragua, where deaf children brought together in new schools created a [[@sign-language|sign language]] with its own grammar in just a few years.

{{story:programming}}

Computers need grammar too, but far stricter than ours. A [[@programming|programming language]] has exact rules, and a single missing bracket can stop a program from running. People, by contrast, understand each other even when sentences are messy, half-finished or full of "umm".

Machine [[@translation|translation]] used to struggle because human grammar is so flexible. Modern systems learn patterns from huge amounts of text instead of following hand-written rules. They can still stumble on a sentence like "Time flies like an arrow; fruit flies like a banana", where the grammar quietly changes halfway through.

That sentence is easy for a ten-year-old and hard for a machine, which says a lot about how good human brains are at grammar.

text: The unicorn began as a travellers' tale, and India sits right at the start of it. Around 400 BCE, a Greek doctor named Ctesias, working at the Persian royal court, wrote about wild animals in India the size of horses, with white bodies and a single long horn. He had never been there. He was probably passing on stories, and many historians think they grew from real animals, especially the one-horned [[@rhino-kaziranga|rhinoceros]].

Later writers repeated and decorated the tale. By the Middle Ages, the unicorn had become a pure white horse with a spiral horn and magical powers. Real objects, like narwhal tusks, made people believe it even more.

st.prompt: In medieval Europe, kings drank from cups said to be made of unicorn horn. What did they believe it would do?

Make them invisible
Help them speak to animals

st.reveal: People believed unicorn horn could detect or cancel poison, so royal families kept "horns" and cups made from them. They were really narwhal tusks, brought from the Arctic by Viking and later traders, and they had no power against poison.

n.certNote: Historians agree that early unicorn stories mixed travellers' tales with real animals such as rhinos. The one-horned animal on Indus seals is still argued over, and nobody can be sure what it meant.

myth: Unicorns were invented for fairy tales and children's toys.
For centuries, educated people in Europe and Asia believed unicorns were real animals living in faraway lands. Natural history books described them alongside lions and elephants.

sec.t:
Ctesias said the horn of the Indian beast could cure poisoning. Later, the Roman writer Pliny the Elder described a "monoceros", meaning one-horn, with a horse's body, an elephant's feet and a deep bellow. That sounds less like a fairy-tale pony and more like a rhino.

The Indian rhino really does have one horn. It lives in grasslands in Assam and Nepal today. Its horn is made of [[keratin|keratin]], the same [[protein|protein]] as your fingernails, not bone. A garbled description passed from trader to trader across Persia and Greece could easily turn a heavy grey animal into something more magical.

sec.h: The one-horned animal on Indus seals

sec.t:
In [[medieval|medieval]] Europe, "unicorn horns" were among the most precious things a king could own. They were long, white and spiralled. They were believed to detect poison, and some were worth more than their weight in gold.

They were really tusks of the narwhal, a whale from the Arctic. A male narwhal's tusk is an overgrown tooth that can grow longer than a tall man is tall. Viking and later traders sold them without explaining their source. Denmark's royal throne, made in the 1600s, is built largely from narwhal tusks. By the 1600s, as more people saw narwhals, scientists began to see through the trick.

sec.h: A unicorn on the royal arms
sec.t:
Scotland adopted the unicorn as a royal symbol in the 1400s, and it is still the country's national animal. In stories, the unicorn was proud and could not be tamed, which suited a kingdom that valued its freedom. When Scotland and England shared a king from 1603, the royal coat of arms showed a lion and a unicorn side by side.

Asia has its own one-horned creatures too. The Chinese qilin, sometimes called a unicorn in English, is a gentle beast whose arrival was said to signal a wise ruler.

Today, unicorns are everywhere: on lunchboxes, cakes and cartoons. In business, a "unicorn" is a young company worth a billion US dollars, a name chosen because such companies were once very rare. India and the USA now have many of them. A unicorn face was added to the official emoji set in 2015, and it quickly became a favourite for birthday messages.

And the strangest part? A giant hairy rhino with a huge single horn, nicknamed the "Siberian unicorn", really did roam Asia until tens of thousands of years ago, at the same time as early humans. Stories of [[@myths-dragons|dragons]] may also have begun with real bones.

text: A poem is writing that pays special attention to sound, [[@rhythm-beat|rhythm]] and shape, as well as meaning. Prose, like this paragraph, runs on until the edge of the page. A poem is usually broken into lines, and the poet decides exactly where each one ends.

Most poems use some of these tools: a beat, rhyme, repeated sounds, vivid pictures in words, and a lot of meaning packed into few words. No one tool is required. Experts have argued for centuries about where poetry stops and prose begins. In the end, a poem is writing that asks you to read slowly and listen.

myth: A poem has to rhyme.
Many poems don't rhyme at all. Most old Sanskrit, Greek and Latin poetry doesn't, and neither do haiku or modern free verse. Rhythm and careful word choice matter more than rhyme.
facts: the epic, such as the Ramayana or the Iliad
poetry without a fixed beat or rhyme

sec.t:
Poetry is older than writing. Before people could write things down, they needed a way to remember laws, prayers, family histories and stories. [[rhythm|Rhythm]] and repetition make words stick in the [[@memory|memory]]. That is why you can recall song lyrics far more easily than a shopping list.

The oldest named author we know of, Enheduanna, was a poet. She was a priestess in the city of Ur in [[@mesopotamia|Mesopotamia]] around 2300 BCE, and hymns carrying her name were copied by scribes for centuries. In India, the hymns of the Rigveda were composed in the [[@vedic-age|Vedic age]] and passed on by heart, in exact rhythms, long before they were written down.

In the south, the Tamil poems of the Sangam period, roughly 2,000 years old, sorted the land into five types: hills, forest, farmland, seashore and dry wasteland. Each landscape went with a mood, such as lovers meeting in the hills or waiting by the sea. A single flower named in a poem could tell readers where they were and how to feel.

**Rhythm** is the pattern of strong and weak beats. [[@sanskrit|Sanskrit]] poets built strict metres, like the shloka, which has four quarters of eight [[syllable|syllables]] each. Tradition says the sage Valmiki spoke the first shloka in grief after seeing a hunter kill a bird, and went on to compose the [[@ramayana|Ramayana]] in that metre.

**Rhyme** is the matching of end sounds, like "moon" and "June". It is common in English, Hindi and Urdu poems and songs.

**Imagery** means pictures made of words. "The fog comes on little cat feet" is the American poet Carl Sandburg's way of showing fog creeping silently in.

**Compression** means saying a lot in a little. A two-line doha by Kabir or a three-line [[@haiku|haiku]] can hold a whole idea.

{{story:hip-hop}}

For most of history, poems were performed aloud, often with music. The [[bhakti|bhakti]] poets [[@mirabai-kabir|Mirabai and Kabir]] composed verses that are still sung in homes and temples across India. [[@ghazals|Ghazals]] in Urdu and Persian are sung at concerts. Many [[@film-songs|film songs]] are poems set to tunes.

Rap is a modern example. [[@hip-hop|Hip-hop]] artists use rhythm, rhyme and wordplay as carefully as any poet, often with rhymes inside lines as well as at the end. Some universities now study rap lyrics alongside older poetry.

In 1855, the American poet Walt Whitman published Leaves of Grass. It used long, loose lines without regular rhyme or metre, a style now called free verse. Many readers were shocked. Today, free verse is probably the most common kind of poem written in English.

Poets keep finding new shapes. Some make "concrete poems", where the words are arranged into a picture. Some write prose poems that look like ordinary paragraphs. Whether something counts as a poem is often settled by how it makes readers listen.

text: Biryani is a dish of fragrant rice layered with spiced meat, fish, eggs or vegetables, then cooked slowly in a sealed pot. Most historians think it grew out of [[@ancient-persia|Persian]] rice dishes like pilaf. Cooks at the courts of the [[@mughals|Mughals]] and the sultans of the Deccan brought them to India from the 1500s onwards.

In India, those dishes met local spices, local rice and local cooks. Over time, every region that took up biryani changed it. That is why there isn't one biryani but dozens. Each tastes of the place where it grew up.

st.prompt: In dum cooking, what do cooks traditionally use to seal the lid of the biryani pot?

options.t: A rope of wheat dough pressed around the rim
Melted wax
Wet clay from a riverbank

st.reveal: A strip of dough is pressed between lid and pot to make an airtight seal. Steam can't escape, so the rice and meat cook slowly in their own juices and smells. When the dough is broken, a cloud of fragrant steam bursts out.

n.certNote: Most food historians link biryani to Persian cooking brought to India by Mughal and Deccan courts. Others point to older Indian rice-and-meat dishes, such as the Tamil oon soru, and to Arab traders on the Kerala coast. No one recipe can be called the first.

myth: Biryani and pulao are the same dish with different names.

They are close cousins. In a pulao, rice and meat or vegetables usually cook together in one go. In a biryani, the rice is usually part-cooked separately and layered with the meat or vegetables, then finished on dum. Cooks argue happily about the exact line.

sec.t:
The word biryani is usually traced to Persian. *Birinj* means rice, and *biryan* means fried or roasted. Persian cooks made pilafs of rice and meat, and these travelled with soldiers, traders and nobles into India.

At royal courts, cooks had time and money to experiment. They added [[@saffron|saffron]], rose water, ghee and many spices. The Mughal court and the courts of the Deccan, especially Golconda near Hyderabad, developed rich, layered rice dishes that became biryani.

Not everyone agrees that biryani came only from Persia. Old Tamil poems describe *oon soru*, rice cooked with meat, ghee and spices, eaten by warriors. Arab traders sailed to the [[@kerala|Kerala]] coast for centuries and brought their own rice dishes.

Some food historians think these older traditions mixed with Persian ideas. Others say they were different dishes that later borrowed the name biryani. Both points of view have supporters, and the evidence isn't enough to settle it. Food and recipes often travel along [[@trade-routes|trade routes]] without leaving clear records.

Biryani's key cooking method is called dum, meaning breath or steam. The meat is marinated in curd and spices, and the rice is partly boiled. They are layered in a heavy pot, sprinkled with saffron milk, fried onions and ghee. The lid is sealed with a rope of dough.

The pot is cooked slowly on low heat, sometimes with hot coals on the lid. Trapped steam finishes cooking the rice and carries the smells of meat and spice through every grain. When the dough seal is broken at the table, the steam rushes out.

Biryani is now one of the most ordered dishes on food delivery apps in India, year after year. It is cooked in huge pots at weddings and at Eid. Vegetarian versions, with [[@cheese-paneer|paneer]], mushrooms or vegetables, are popular too, though some people insist that only pulao can be vegetarian.

Biryani has followed Indians, Pakistanis and Bangladeshis around the world. You'll find it in Dubai, London, Toronto and New Jersey. There it is cooked by families from many regions, each sure that their grandmother's [[@rice|rice]] is the best.

text: Guavas and papayas first grew in the warm forests of southern Mexico, Central America and northern South America. People there were eating them long before Europeans arrived.

After [[@columbus|Columbus]] crossed the Atlantic in 1492, Spanish and [[@portuguese-india|Portuguese]] sailors carried American plants around the world. Guavas and papayas travelled across oceans along with chillies, tomatoes, potatoes and corn. They probably reached India in the 1500s and 1600s, and loved the warm [[climate|climate]] so much that they grew almost everywhere. Today India grows more guavas and more papayas than any other country.

a giant herb, not a true tree

sec.t:
Guava trees are small and tough. They grow in poor soil, survive dry spells and fruit twice a year. Their fruit can be white or pink inside, packed with small hard seeds, and smells strongly sweet when ripe.

In India, guava is called amrood or peru in many places. Street sellers slice it and sprinkle it with salt and red chilli powder, which makes the sweet fruit taste even sweeter. Prayagraj, formerly Allahabad, is famous for a variety called Allahabad Safeda.

Weight for weight, guava has about four times as much [[@vitamins|vitamin C]] as an orange. Your body needs [[vitamin|vitamin]] C to heal cuts and keep gums healthy, and it can't store much, so you need some every day.

A papaya plant looks like a palm tree, but it isn't a tree at all. It is a giant herb with a soft, hollow stem and a crown of big leaves at the top. It can grow from a seed to a fruiting plant in less than a year, which is very fast for a plant that size.

Papaya fruit hangs in clusters right under the leaves. Inside, the flesh is orange and soft, with a hollow full of shiny black seeds that taste peppery. Green papaya is cooked as a vegetable or grated into salads in many parts of India and Southeast Asia.

Unripe papaya is full of an [[enzyme|enzyme]] called papain, which breaks down [[protein|proteins]]. Cooks in India have long added raw papaya paste to meat to make it tender, and papain is used in some meat tenderiser powders.

In the 1990s, a virus called papaya ringspot spread through papaya farms in [[@hawaii-culture|Hawaii]]. It made the plants weak and the fruit spotty, and the industry was close to collapse. Scientists at the University of Hawaii and Cornell University developed a papaya that resists the virus by giving it a small piece of the virus's own [[gene|genes]], a little like a [[vaccine|vaccine]].

Farmers began planting this "Rainbow" papaya in 1998, and Hawaiian papaya farming recovered. It is one of the best-known examples of a genetically modified crop helping farmers, though people still debate whether such crops should be grown.

Both fruits now grow wild in many [[tropical|tropical]] places they weren't native to. Guava trees spread so well that they have become a weed in some islands, crowding out local plants. In India, though, they mostly stay in gardens, orchards and street carts. It's strange to think that a fruit sold from a handcart outside an Indian school first ripened in a forest on the other side of the world.
